To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) job satisfaction and job satisfaction measures are correlated with job performance, (2) job performance is not correlated with wages or wages growth, (3) the correlation between job satisfaction and wages is negative, (4) job satisfaction is correlated with interest in the job, (5) job satisfaction is not correlated with job autonomy, (6) the correlation between interest in the job and job satisfaction is positive and significant, (7) interest in the job is correlated with wages and job satisfaction,

job satisfaction is positively correlated with intrinsic motivations and with self-esteem, and that job performance is positively correlated with both intrinsic motivations and selfesteem, and negatively correlated with extrinsic motivations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: What do we mean by job satisfaction?
the following question: what are the factors that affect job satisfaction and performance?
the relationship between job satisfaction and job productivity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
job performance is positively correlated with job satisfac-tion, but that this correlation is not as strong as the one between job performance and interest in the job.
the empirical evidence on the relation between job satisfaction and job satisfaction and job productivity is mixed and inconclusive.
the evidence from the empirical studies reviewed here is not consistent with the hypothesis that the main determinants of job performance are economic incentives.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the empirical evidence is consistent with the idea that the employer can use other means, besides using incentives, to motivate employees.
the economic analysis of job performance is still in its infancy and that there are a number of issues that have been neglected by economists.

the empirical evidence on the relationship between job performance and job satisfaction, as well as on the effects of monetary rewards on performance, is not consistent with the predictions of standard economic theory.
The main takeaway from our work is that
job performance is a function of job satisfaction.
the economic theory of the firm is not yet fully equipped to explain the empirical evidence on the relationship between job performance and job satisfaction.
job satisfaction and performance are positively correlated, and that the employer should take this into account in order to increase the performance of his employees.
